verdicts.trueWording: “Kay’s novels stand out for their richness of character, their fullness of scene”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200, brightweavings.com). Gunn's Easton Press introduction, signed 'James Gunn, Lawrence, Kansas, July 30, 1998'. Sentence reads in full: 'Kay’s novels stand out for their richness of character, their fullness of scene, and particularly for their realism of situation and action.' Quote and every limb of the claim supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “Tigana reads like a richly tapestried historical novel dense with character and detail”
verdicts.note: Same raw page. Full sentence: 'Tigana reads like a richly tapestried historical novel dense with character and detail, but it occurs in a world the reader does not know, a world with two moons, one white, one blue.' Quote verbatim; claim's wording tracks the page exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: “willingness to kill off major characters … gives the edge of reality”
verdicts.note: Same raw page: 'Kay surprises his readers by his willingness to kill off major characters, even his most attractive ones, and this, too, gives the edge of reality to what might otherwise be airily fantastic.' Sentence sits inside the Tigana paragraph, so the 'gives Tigana the edge of reality' limb is supported by context as well as wording.

verdicts.trueWording: “Kay’s work offers an enrichment for its readers that is primarily emotional rather than rational”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Byline confirms 'by Christopher Cobb … First published in Foundation, Summer 2005.' Page says 'Kay's work' where the claim says 'Kay's historical fantasy'; the essay's whole subject is Kay's historical/parallel-world fantasy, and the surrounding sentences ('Kay's treatment of history in his fantasies'), so the limb is supported, not merely adjacent.

verdicts.trueWording: “the past cannot be changed, but history – the memory and the record of the past – can … be changed”
verdicts.note: Same raw page, in the Tigana section ('This magical vengeance makes Tigana into a meditation on the psychological importance of remembered and shared history'). Full sentence: 'As in Fionavar's Arthur story, the past cannot be changed, but history – the memory and the record of the past – can most definitely and most destructively be changed.' Every limb, including the 'in Tigana' framing and the gloss 'the memory and the record of the past', is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “the plottings are those of political survival ungarlanded by personal myth”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Byline: 'by Janeen Webb … first appeared in The New York Review of Science Fiction, No.77, January 1995.' Full sentence: 'While mythic conflations produced Tigana's characterisations, the process in A Song for Arbonne is an historical one. This is a less innocent, more secular text, where the plottings are those of political survival ungarlanded by personal myth.' The contrast with Tigana is explicit in the preceding clause.

verdicts.trueWording: “whose voice at times resembles that of a historian in its distanced relation of events”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200); header confirms 'the 2012 honours thesis by Matthew Rettino written when while attending McGill University'. Full sentence: 'Kay's narrator, whose voice at times resembles that of a historian in its distanced relation of events, can be understood to be operating according to club-story assumptions.' Sits in the Tigana/club-story section (the following example is Duke Sandre), matching the cited page location.

verdicts.trueWording: “The narrator presents himself as one Kitan historian among many.”
verdicts.note: Same raw thesis page, in the Under Heaven section: 'Kay's narrator is not only a historian, but is implicitly the creator of a fantasy about history. The narrator presents himself as one Kitan historian among many.' Quotation is a complete verbatim sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: “The narrator subtly offers information to the reader, disguising it as Jehane’s thoughts.”
verdicts.note: Same raw thesis page, in the Lions of Al-Rassan section. The passage first shows narratorial prose following Jehane's reflection, then concludes: 'The narrator subtly offers information to the reader, disguising it as Jehane's thoughts.' Quote verbatim (truncated mid-phrase in the claim record); all limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: “several scenes in this novel where a conversation takes place, as described by more than one of the people”
verdicts.note: Raw LARB page fetched (HTTP 200); byline 'By Christine Fischer Guy, August 14, 2016'. Kay: 'I have several scenes in this novel where a conversation takes place, as described by more than one of the people in the conversation.' 'This novel' is Children of Earth and Sky, the book under discussion throughout the interview.

verdicts.trueWording: “When I switch to another character’s point of view, the conversation isn’t the same.”
verdicts.note: Same raw LARB page, immediately following the sentence behind index 189: 'When I switch to another character's point of view, the conversation isn't the same. It bears a resemblance, but it's not the same.' Quotation verbatim including the curly apostrophe.

verdicts.trueWording: “it takes place on the borderlands in the lives of not-powerful people”
verdicts.note: Same raw LARB page: 'One of the starting points of this book in my own mind was that it takes place on the borderlands in the lives of not-powerful people.' The answer is the one about honouring fathers' legacies, in which Kay also raises the ghosts of the recently dead, matching the cited location.

verdicts.trueWording: “You can have a forgotten emperor and the chronicler of the reign is remembered.”
verdicts.note: Same raw LARB page, answering the interviewer's prompt 'There are examples of art that has endured after empires have fallen.' Kay: 'Yes, that's the point, that there's no single template. You can have a forgotten emperor and the chronicler of the reign is remembered.' Both limbs — art outlasting power, and the emperor/chronicler example — are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “The narrator often refers to places without explaining where they are located … creates a feeling of reading a historical text with geographical references”
verdicts.note: PDF fetched as binary (HTTP 200, 301,329 bytes) and text extracted with pypdf, 18 pages. Header confirms 'Petra Pugar, University of Zagreb' in the journal 'Words to Works'. The sentence falls after the running header 'Words to Works 168' and under the heading 'Geographical map as a paratext', so p. 168 and the section are both right. The page adds a middle limb the claim omits ('almost forcing the reader to return to the map'), which strengthens rather than contradicts the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: “persuading the implied reader that they are dealing with a true account, giving evidence of the past”
verdicts.note: Same extracted PDF text. Passage discusses the prologue — Saevar on the riverbank, 'the first focalizer in the novel', and the next sentence begins 'After the prologue, the reader discovers…' — so the 'prologue' limb is supported. The sentence sits before the running header 'Words to Works 166', i.e. on p. 165 as cited.
